Can we safely divide this problem?

CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 14 / 54

Parallel design is not just “add threads”.

Wrong partition

Some workers may receive too much work while others finish early.

Hidden dependency

One task may need the result of another task.

Too much communication

Workers may spend more time talking than computing.

Poor mapping

Tasks may not match processor/memory structure.

CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 15 / 54

A good parallel design answers four questions.

1What can be divided?Find independent or mostly independent work.
2What must communicate?Identify information exchanged between tasks.
3What should be grouped?Reduce unnecessary task and communication overhead.
4Where should work run?Assign tasks to processors or workers.
These four questions lead naturally to PCAM.

P — Partitioning

Partitioning means dividing the original problem into smaller pieces of work.

  • Data blocks
  • Image regions
  • Matrix rows or columns
  • Pipeline stages

Functional decomposition divides the work by function.

ReadParseAnalyzeStoreAlert
Different tasks perform different operations, often as a pipeline.
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 113 / 54

Two common decomposition views

AspectDomain DecompositionFunctional Decomposition
Main ideaDivide dataDivide operations
Typical patternSame work on data blocksDifferent tasks/stages
ExampleImage regionsCapture → Parse → Detect
Related modelData parallelTask parallel
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 114 / 54

Choose domain or functional decomposition

Scenario 1: Apply the same malware hash check to one million files.
Likely: Domain decomposition / data parallel.
Scenario 2: Receive packets, decode packets, run detection, then generate alerts.
Likely: Functional decomposition / task parallel.
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 115 / 54

Dependencies: what must wait for what?

Task A
read data
→
Task B
analyze
→
Task C
report
A dependency exists when one task requires the output or completion of another task.
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 116 / 54

Parallelism exists when tasks can proceed independently.

Independent

Worker 1 scans block A.

Worker 2 scans block B.

No need to wait during scanning.

Dependent

Task B needs Task A output.

Task C needs Task B output.

Parallelism is limited.

CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 117 / 54

Think → Predict

Problem: Find maximum in four independent data blocks, then compare four local maxima.
Step 1

Can local maxima run in parallel?

Yes. Each block is independent.
Step 2

Can final maximum run before local maxima finish?

No. It depends on all local results.
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 118 / 54

Granularity: how large is each task?

Fine-grained

Many small tasks.

High management and communication overhead.

Coarse-grained

Fewer larger tasks.

Less overhead, but possible load imbalance.

Good design chooses task size carefully.
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 119 / 54

Fine-grained: many tiny tasks

Good for exposing parallelism, but overhead can dominate.
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 120 / 54

Coarse-grained: fewer larger tasks

Block 1Block 2Block 3Block 4
Good for reducing overhead, but tasks must remain balanced.
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 121 / 54

Choosing granularity is a trade-off

ChoiceStrengthRisk
Fine-grainedMore possible parallelismMore overhead and communication
Coarse-grainedLower overheadPossible load imbalance
BalancedGood throughputRequires problem understanding
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 122 / 54

Choose the better granularity

Scenario: 10 million log records and 4 CPU cores.
A

One task per log record.

B

Four large blocks, one per core.

C

Random tiny groups with frequent communication.

Best starting point: B, because overhead is lower and blocks can be balanced.

PCAM starts with partitioning

Original problem

Partition

Local work

Dependency

C — Communication

Communication means identifying data that must move between tasks.

  • Input values
  • Intermediate results
  • Boundary data
  • Final partial results

CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 231 / 54

Communication can be local or global

Local communication

Nearby or neighboring tasks exchange data.

Example: image boundary pixels.

Global communication

Many tasks communicate with one task or all tasks.

Example: reduction to final maximum.

CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 232 / 54

Communication is not free

Latency

Delay before data arrives.

Bandwidth

Amount of data moved per time.

Synchronization

Waiting for others to finish.

CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 233 / 54

Board Activity: Identify the communication

Scenario: Four groups process four blocks of risk scores. Each group finds one local maximum.
1. Write your group’s local maximum.
2. Decide what must be sent to the final group.
3. Decide whether communication is local or global.
Expected: Send only local maxima; final reduction is global communication.
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 234 / 54

A — Agglomeration

Agglomeration means grouping small tasks into larger tasks.

Purpose: reduce overhead and improve practical performance.

↓
Group 1Group 2Group 3Group 4
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 235 / 54

Too many tiny tasks can be inefficient

Task overhead

Creating and scheduling many tiny tasks costs time.

Communication overhead

Tiny tasks may exchange too many messages.

Poor cache locality

Small scattered tasks may reduce locality.

Harder management

More tasks make mapping and debugging difficult.

CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 236 / 54

Before and after grouping

Before

One task per data item.

16 tiny tasks.

After

One task per block.

4 useful tasks.

Agglomeration often converts fine-grained tasks into practical coarse-grained tasks.
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 237 / 54

Think → Decide

You have 1,000,000 risk scores and 4 cores. Initial partitioning creates 1,000,000 tiny tasks.

Should we keep one task per score?

No. Group scores into larger blocks so each core receives a useful amount of work.
Reason: fewer tasks, lower scheduling overhead, better locality.
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 238 / 54

M — Mapping

Mapping assigns tasks to processors or workers.

A good mapping tries to:

  • balance workload;
  • reduce communication;
  • use available hardware effectively.
Task 1
Task 2
Task 3
Task 4
Core 1Core 2Core 3Core 4
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 239 / 54

Good mapping keeps workers busy

If one worker receives much more work, other workers wait at the join point.
CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 240 / 54

Three mapping goals

Balance

Keep all processors similarly busy.

Locality

Place tasks near the data they use.

Low communication

Avoid unnecessary data movement between workers.

CS-426 · Week 05 · Theory Session 241 / 54

Group Mapping Challenge

Dataset sizes: Block A = 100, Block B = 100, Block C = 100, Block D = 500

How would you map these blocks to four cores?

Discuss: is the workload balanced?

Observation: Simple one-block-per-core mapping is imbalanced because Block D is much larger.
Improvement: split Block D or use dynamic scheduling if possible.

End-to-end PCAM for parallel maximum

1PartitionSplit data into four blocks.
2CommunicateSend four local maxima to final reducer.
3AgglomerateUse block-level tasks instead of one task per item.
4MapAssign one block to each core.
Final maximum = 96

Avoid these mistakes

Mistake 1

Calling partitioning and mapping the same thing.

Mistake 2

Ignoring communication cost.

Mistake 3

Creating too many tiny tasks.

Mistake 4

Assuming equal number of cores always means equal speedup.
